lead: Micro actuators make controlled motion on the scale of micrometres: a valve opens, a mirror tilts, a droplet leaves a nozzle. They exist because coils and magnets do not shrink well; a tiny coil has few turns and high resistance, so magnetic force falls away. Three common families use piezoelectric strain, shape-memory phase change, or electrostatic attraction. You meet them in inkjet print heads, micropumps, RF MEMS switches, the self-test actuator inside some accelerometers, and micro mirrors.
prereq: You need piezoelectric transducers and MEMS micromachining; see pneumatic and hydraulic actuators for the macro fluid-power contrast.

blocks.text: The inverse piezoelectric effect is the useful half of the story. Apply an electric field across a poled piezoelectric ceramic and it changes shape. The strain is small but the force is large and the response is fast. A PZT plate can reach about 0.1% strain; a 100 µm length therefore moves about 0.1 µm. That is enough for fine positioning but not for a long stroke.

blocks.where: S is strain (ΔL/L, no unit); d<sub>33</sub> is the piezoelectric charge coefficient in m/V, often quoted in pm/V; E is the electric field in V/m. For PZT, d<sub>33</sub> is a few hundred pm/V, and the data sheet value depends on the ceramic and its poling.

blocks.text: A stack actuator puts many thin ceramic layers mechanically in series and electrically in parallel. The same low voltage drives every layer, and the small strains add, so the stack gives a larger stroke and a high stiffness. A bimorph is two piezo layers on a thin beam; one expands while the other contracts, and the beam bends. A bimorph gives a larger tip deflection at lower force. Both types can run at kHz rates.

items: Inkjet print head: a piezo element squeezes an ink chamber and shoots a drop.
Micropump: a piezo disc flexes a diaphragm.
Precision positioning: stacks hold optical parts without gears.

sections.h3: Shape memory alloy: strain from phase change

blocks.text: A shape memory alloy (SMA) changes crystal phase with temperature. Below a transition temperature it is in martensite, which is soft and can be deformed. Heat it and it becomes austenite, and it returns to its remembered shape. The recoverable strain is large, typically 4% to 8%, far more than piezo strain. The force per volume is also high.

The catch is heat. A small SMA wire is heated by passing current, but cooling is by conduction and convection into the surroundings. Cooling is slow, so a simple SMA actuator may cycle at only a few hertz or less. The phase change also has hysteresis: the heating and cooling curves do not coincide. For repeated motion, a bias spring or a second wire pulls the actuator back.

items: Wire or film: NiTi is common; a 50 µm wire can be Joule-heated.
Microgripper: two SMA arms close when heated.
Microvalve: an SMA plug opens a flow channel.
Limit: slow cooling, hysteresis and fatigue set the cycle life.

blocks.text: Nitinol (NiTi) is the medical shape memory alloy. A self-expanding stent is crimped small and cold, slid through a catheter, and opens to its remembered diameter at body temperature; the same alloy makes kink-resistant guidewires and orthodontic arch wires that pull teeth with a steady force. Piezo micropumps deliver insulin and drugs, and piezo elements are the heart of every ultrasound probe.

Two conducting plates with a gap form a capacitor. Apply a voltage and the plates attract. The capacitance is C = ε<sub>0</sub> A / g, where ε<sub>0</sub> is the permittivity of free space (8.854 × 10<sup>−12</sup> F/m), A is the overlap area in m², and g is the gap in m. The stored energy is U = CV²/2. At constant applied voltage the force is +∂U/∂x with x measured along the closing direction, which gives the formula below; at constant charge the sign flips but the magnitude is the same. Here x is displacement in m and U is stored energy in J.

blocks.where: F is force in N; V is applied voltage in V; ε<sub>0</sub> is 8.854 × 10<sup>−12</sup> F/m; A is area in m²; g is gap in m. The force goes as V², so reversing the voltage does not reverse the force.

blocks.text: A parallel-plate actuator is simple but has pull-in. As the plate moves, g falls and F rises as 1/g². With g0 the initial gap, the spring force rises linearly with displacement x = g0 − g, that is, as the gap g falls. Beyond x = g0/3 (remaining gap 2g0/3) the electrostatic force grows faster than the spring can balance and the plates snap together; a simple voltage control cannot hold a stable position past that point.

A comb drive avoids that in its travel direction. Interlocking fingers change overlap area, not gap, so the force is nearly constant with position. Comb drives still need tens of volts because the gaps are small and the capacitance is only picofarads. They are common in micro mirrors and resonant sensors.

sections.h3: Magnetic, fluidic and where micro actuators are used

blocks.text: Magnetic micro actuation uses a coil or a thin magnetic film. At small scale a coil has few turns and high resistance, so the force is modest and the drive current is high. Magnetic actuation still appears where a large throw or a bistable latch is needed; for coils at macro scale see solenoids, relays and motors. Fluidic micro actuation uses pressure in a channel to push a membrane or a plug. It gives a large force, but it needs valves, seals and a pressure source.

items: RF MEMS switch: an electrostatic or piezo beam closes a radio-frequency contact; low loss and low power when held.
Micro mirror: a torsion plate tilts under electrostatic force; arrays steer light in displays and scanners.
Micropump and inkjet: piezo or electrostatic drive moves a diaphragm.

figure.caption: A 200 µm square plate 2 µm above a fixed electrode feels 39.8 µN at 30 V. The electric force rises as 1/(g₀ − x)², the spring force in a straight line; at the pull-in voltage they touch at x = g₀/3, so past 0.667 µm the plate snaps down.

spec.aria: A movable plate hung on two springs above a fixed electrode with a 30 volt cell between them, a 2 micrometre gap and a dashed pull-in line after 0.667 micrometres; a graph of normalised force against travel with a straight spring line and three electric force curves, below, at and above the pull-in voltage, the middle one tangent at one third of the gap.

examples.question: A parallel-plate electrostatic micro actuator has a square plate 200 µm × 200 µm, a gap of 2 µm and an applied voltage of 30 V. Take ε<sub>0</sub> = 8.854 × 10<sup>−12</sup> F/m. Find the capacitance, the electrostatic force, and the displacement at which pull-in occurs, together with the remaining gap at that point.
steps: Voltage V = 30 V, so V² = 900 V² and g² = 4 × 10<sup>−12</sup> m².
Pull-in occurs when the plate has moved one third of the initial gap: displacement = g0/3 = (2 µm)/3 = 0.667 µm, so the remaining gap is 2g0/3 = 1.33 µm.
examples.answer: Capacitance is about 0.177 pF, electrostatic force is about 39.8 µN, and pull-in occurs after 0.667 µm of travel, at a remaining gap of about 1.33 µm.
examples.check:
eps = 8.854e-12
A = (200e-6) ** 2
g = 2e-6
V = 30
C = eps * A / g
F = eps * A * V**2 / (2 * g**2)
disp_pull = g / 3
g_remaining = 2 * g / 3
print(round(C * 1e12, 3))
print(round(F * 1e6, 1))
print(round(disp_pull * 1e6, 3))
print(round(g_remaining * 1e6, 3))

examples.question: A piezo stack has 100 PZT layers, each 0.1 mm thick, with d<sub>33</sub> = 500 pm/V, driven at 100 V. A NiTi wire 50 mm long recovers 4 % strain. Find (a) the field in each layer, (b) the stroke of one layer and of the stack, (c) the stack strain, and (d) the SMA stroke, and compare.
steps: (a) Each layer has the full 100 V across 0.1 mm: E = 100 / (0.1 × 10⁻³) = 1.0 × 10⁶ V/m.
(b) One layer: ΔL = d<sub>33</sub> V = 500 × 10⁻¹² × 100 = 5.0 × 10⁻⁸ m = 50 nm (strain d<sub>33</sub>E times thickness gives the same). The stack adds 100 layers: 5.0 µm.
(c) Stack length = 100 × 0.1 mm = 10 mm, so strain = 5.0 µm / 10 mm = 5 × 10⁻⁴ = 0.05 %.
Check: the SMA stroke is 2.0 mm / 5.0 µm = 400 times the stack's, but the stack responds in microseconds while the wire needs seconds to cool, which is why each is used where it is.
examples.answer: The field is 1.0 MV/m; a layer moves 50 nm and the stack 5.0 µm (0.05 % strain); the SMA wire moves 2.0 mm.

traps: Do not use the direct piezoelectric effect when asked how a piezo actuator moves; actuation uses the inverse effect: voltage in, strain out.
Pull-in occurs after the plate has moved one third of the initial gap, so the remaining gap is two thirds of the initial gap (not half); beyond that displacement voltage control is unstable.
SMA recoverable strain is 4–8% of length, not 4–8 µm; check whether the question gives a wire length.

quiz.q: Define the inverse piezoelectric effect and name one micro-actuator use.
quiz.a: An applied electric field produces strain in a poled piezoelectric material. One use is a piezo inkjet print head or micropump.

quiz.q: Why are coils and magnets less suitable for micro actuators?
quiz.a: At small size a coil has few turns and high resistance, so it gives little force for its current. Magnets and coils are also hard to integrate with planar micromachining.

quiz.q: A parallel-plate electrostatic actuator has area 100 µm × 100 µm, gap 1.5 µm and voltage 20 V. Take ε<sub>0</sub> = 8.854 × 10<sup>−12</sup> F/m. Find the force.
Explain why a simple voltage control cannot hold a parallel-plate actuator once the plate has moved beyond one third of the initial gap.
quiz.a: As the gap falls, electrostatic force rises as 1/g² while the spring force rises linearly with displacement x = g0 − g, where g0 is the initial gap; that is, the spring force rises as the gap g falls. Past a displacement of g0/3 (remaining gap 2g0/3) the electrostatic force grows faster, so any small further movement increases force more than the spring can balance; the plates snap together.

quiz.q: An electrostatic actuator force is proportional to V². If the voltage is doubled, by what factor does the force change?

beyond: Not for the exam. Thin-film PZT ultrasonic transducers (pMUTs) are used in fingerprint and ultrasound sensing, and RF MEMS switches in tunable radio front ends. Search pMUT and RF MEMS ohmic switch.
